scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

In professional contexts, a suit may enhance confidence, while in informal settings, it might not have the same effect. 7. **Personal Experience**: Individual experiences and feelings about wearing a suit play a role, as some may feel empowered while others constricted. In conclusion, confidence from wearing a suit arises from a blend of how others perceive you, your self-perception, psychological associations, comfort, social norms, context, and personal experiences.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to lie to my brother about having a disorder, specifically Asperger's, just to make him feel better and help him move forward in life. Let me break this down step by step. First, I need to understand the situation fully. My brother has Asperger's, which is a form of autism. He's extremely smart, excels in math and physics, and is doing well in college. However, he's been really depressed, to the point where he tried to take his own life a few months ago. He's been in outpatient treatment after being discharged from inpatient care. He's very close to me and only talks to me about these things. Recently, a nurse asked me if my brother was diagnosed with autism because she noticed some signs. I talked to him about it, but he's still denying that he has autism. He's embarrassed about it, even though he's so intelligent and capable. I've tried to talk to him about not being ashamed and owning his disorder, but it doesn't seem to help. I mentioned that people like Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs are thought to have Asperger's, but that didn't make a difference either. Now, I'm considering lying to him about having Asperger's myself, thinking that if he knows I have it too, he might feel less alone and possibly stop denying his own diagnosis. But I'm wondering if that's the right thing to do. Would I be an asshole for lying to him like that? Let me think about the possible outcomes of this lie. On one hand, if he feels less alone and more accepted, he might start to embrace his diagnosis and seek the help he needs. That could be really beneficial for him, especially given his history of depression and the recent suicide attempt. On the other hand, lying to him could damage our trust relationship. If he finds out that I lied to him, he might feel betrayed, which could strain our relationship. Plus, lying about having a disorder that I don't actually have could be seen as trivializing his experience. Disorders like Asperger's are real and can have significant impacts on people's lives, so pretending to have one when I don't might not be respectful. I also need to consider the ethical implications of lying. Generally, honesty is valued in relationships because it builds trust and respect. Lying can erode those foundations, even if the intention is to help. There's also the question of whether the potential benefits of the lie outweigh the risks of betrayal and mistrust. Maybe there's another way to help him without lying. Instead of pretending to have Asperger's, I could find other ways to support him emotionally. I could continue to have open and honest conversations with him about his feelings and struggles. I could also look for resources or support groups that might help him feel less alone and more understood. It's also important to think about his long-term well-being. If he continues to deny his diagnosis, he might not seek the help he needs, which could lead to further mental health issues. Encouraging him to embrace his identity and seek appropriate support could be more effective in the long run than trying to make him feel better by lying. In summary, while the intention behind lying to my brother is to help him feel less alone and encourage him to embrace his diagnosis, the potential negative consequences of lying, such as damaging our trust and trivializing his experience, seem significant. It might be better to approach the situation with honesty and find other ways to support him without resorting to deception.
